Opportunities for international collaboration and conference presentations.
Training in simulation, experimental techniques, and project management.
Skills development for both academic and industrial career pathways.
Advanced Artificial Intelligence Techniques for Discovery of New Superconductors
Supervisors: Dr Mohammad Yazdani-Asrami
Project Overview
Superconductors are remarkable materials that can conduct electricity with zero resistance below a certain critical temperature, enabling ultra-efficient power transmission, high-field fusion magnets, and transformative technologies in energy, healthcare, and transportation. However, most currently known superconductors require extremely low operating temperatures or expensive, rare materials, which limits their scalability and affordability. High-temperature superconductors, while promising, still face challenges in manufacturability, mechanical robustness, and consistent performance under real-world operating conditions. These limitations constrain widespread deployment in critical sectors such as fusion energy, and next-generation transportation systems.
To unlock the full potential of superconductivity, there is an urgent need to discover new superconducting materials with higher critical temperatures, improved mechanical properties, and cost-effective composition. Conventional experimental trial-and-error approaches are time-consuming and extremely resource-intensive, while traditional computational methods struggle with the complexity of strongly correlated systems. Recent advances in Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Deep Learning (DL) offer a transformative pathway—by rapidly screening vast chemical spaces, learning from incomplete datasets, and uncovering hidden structure–property relationships, AI can dramatically accelerate the search and optimisation of novel superconductors.
This PhD program will focus on developing and applying advanced AI techniques—such as deep generative models, physics-informed neural networks, and reinforcement learning—for the accelerated discovery of new superconductors, potentially those of near room temperature. The research will integrate domain knowledge from materials physics, quantum chemistry, and condensed matter theory with state-of-the-art AI algorithms to predict superconducting properties, guide synthesis, and identify candidate materials with unprecedented efficiency. The work will involve close collaboration with experimental and computational research groups (from France and USA) and superconductor manufacturer (from Japan, Germany) to validate predictions and feed new data into the discovery pipeline.

Advanced Multiphysics Electro-magneto-thermo-mechanical Modelling of Superconductors for Future Energy Systems
Supervisors: Dr Wenjuan Song and Dr Mohammad Yazdani-Asrami
Project Overview
Superconductors, are poised to revolutionise the way that energy will be generated, transmitted, and stored in future, offering lossless electrical transport, ultra-compact and powerful magnets, and highly efficient devices for medical, power, and transport applications. Superconductors’ ability to operate at high current densities and magnetic fields makes them critical enablers for future energy systems such as fusion reactors, large-scale renewable energy integration, high-speed transportation, and advanced power grid. Examples are superconducting propulsion motor for hydrogen powered aircraft, superconducting cables for electric power system, superconducting magnet for fusion energy generation, and superconducting transformer for high speed trains. With the pressing global need to decarbonise and improve energy efficiency, superconducting technologies promise transformative impacts on sustainability, reliability, and performance.
Despite these benefits, designing superconducting components for real-world applications is an immensely complex task due to the intricate coupling of electromagnetic, thermal, and mechanical phenomena under extreme operating conditions. Superconductors exhibit highly non-linear material behaviour, anisotropic properties, and strong dependencies on temperature, magnetic field, and strain. Modelling these systems requires the simultaneous solution of Maxwell’s equations, heat transfer dynamics, and mechanical stress–strain responses — all of which interact in a Multiphysics loop. Achieving accurate, predictive, and computationally efficient models remains a significant scientific and engineering challenge, especially when scaling from laboratory prototypes to industrial systems.
This successful PhD will focus on developing advanced Multiphysics electro-magneto-thermo-mechanical modelling tools tailored for next-generation superconducting devices in future energy systems. The research will integrate finite-element simulations, high-fidelity material characterisation, novel computational techniques and artificial intelligence and machine learning to capture the coupled physics with unprecedented accuracy. Application areas may include superconducting power cables, high-field magnets, fault-current limiters, and superconducting machines. The successful candidate will work closely with academic and industry partners, contributing to both fundamental modelling advances and practical design optimisation, paving the way for safer, more reliable, and higher-performing superconducting technologies.

Grey-box Digital Twin Framework for Advanced Air Mobility Self-Certification
Supervisor: Dr. Ye Yuan
Project Overview
Advanced Air Mobility (AAM) promises to revolutionise urban and regional transportation, significantly reducing ground congestion. Despite the rapid technological advancements, airworthiness certification remains a major barrier, primarily due to cost-prohibitive traditional certification methods involving extensive, risky, and expensive flight testing. Digital twin technology, which creates virtual representations of physical systems, offers the potential to transform the certification landscape through self-certification. However, current approaches rely on black-box, data-driven models that lack transparency, interpretability, and scalability. There is an urgent need for more interpretable, physics-informed digital twins that align seamlessly with formal regulatory compliance processes.
This PhD project will develop a novel grey-box digital twin framework designed explicitly for probabilistic self-certification of AAM vehicles. The digital twin will leverage physics-informed and data-driven approaches to provide interpretable, generalisable, and scalable models.
Specifically, the research objectives are to:
Develop a probabilistic grey-box digital twin framework that integrates existing rotorcraft physics models, Bayesian inference techniques, and multi-agent system enabling characterisation of flight dynamics, propulsion/motor systems, pilot/autonomous controls, and potential airspace interactions.
Implement advanced probabilistic methods, including Fault Tree Analysis (FTA) combined with Bayesian inference, to estimate joint failure probabilities, capturing interdependencies and realistic statistical correlations.
Train the developed digital twin through extensive computational simulations (such as CFD results) and field experiments conducted at the University of Glasgow's UAV test facility.
Candidate Profile
The ideal candidate will possess:
An MSc or MEng degree (or equivalent) primarily in Aerospace Engineering. Applicants from related fields such as Mechanical Engineering, Computational Science, Control Engineering, Data Science, or Applied Mathematics who demonstrate a strong interest in aerospace applications and advanced air mobility are also encouraged to apply.
Demonstrated knowledge or keen interest in digital twin technologies and probabilistic modelling.
Strong computational skills, including familiarity with simulation software and programming languages commonly used in probabilistic modelling and aerodynamics simulations.
Enthusiasm for interdisciplinary research and collaboration, with an interest in shaping future regulatory frameworks and industrial practices in advanced air mobility.

Integrating Advanced Aerodynamics Modelling with Autonomous UAV Systems for Offshore Wind Turbine Monitoring
Supervisor: Dr. Ye Yuan
Project Overview
The use of Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) for inspecting operational offshore wind turbines holds great potential for reducing downtime, lowering maintenance costs, and improving safety. However, significant challenges remain due to complex aerodynamic interactions between UAVs and rotating turbine blades, adversely affecting UAV stability and inspection accuracy. This PhD project, collaborating with Offshore Renewable Energy Catapult, aims to integrate advanced aerodynamic models with autonomous control systems to enhance UAV performance during operational turbine inspections.
The successful candidate will focus on:
Integrating a state-of-the-art aerodynamic interaction model (Ring-Type Vortex Wake, RTVW) with a Multi-Timestep Inverse Simulation (MTIS)-based autonomous control system to ensure stable UAV operation close to rotating turbine blades.
Enhancing computational efficiency of the integrated RTVW-MTIS framework through advanced methods, such as harmonic decomposition, to achieve real-time operational feasibility.
Conducting experimental validation and gaining hands-on experience through wind tunnel, verifying model predictions and autonomous system performance under realistic aerodynamic conditions.
Candidate Profile
The ideal candidate will possess:
A strong academic background primarily in Aerospace Engineering, though candidates from Mechanical Engineering, Computational Science, or Control Engineering with a keen interest in aerospace applications are also encouraged to apply.
Experience or strong interest in aerodynamics, autonomous systems, numerical modelling, and simulation.
